interactive.title: The impedance builder
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the complex plane from the earlier lessons, real across and j up, with every length in ohms. The builder lays three arrows tip to tail from 0: the resistor's R along the real axis, then the coil's +jX_L straight up from its tip, then the capacitor's −jX_C straight down from there. The arrow from 0 to the last tip, drawn bold, is the impedance Z = R + j(X_L − X_C), with its angle φ drawn as an arc from the positive real axis. Readouts give Z in parts and as a length and an angle, and cos φ, the power factor. On some screens four sliders set the resistance R (0 to 20 Ω), the coil's inductance L (0 to 40 mH), the capacitor's capacitance C (100 to 1000 µF) and the frequency f (20 to 150 Hz). The coil's reactance is X_L = 2πfL and the capacitor's is X_C = 1 ÷ (2πfC), with L in henries and C in farads, so raising f lengthens the coil's arrow in step with f and shortens the capacitor's. A small wave panel, a sketch, shows a coil's current and its voltage as two waves a quarter cycle apart, the voltage peaking first, because a coil's voltage follows how fast its current changes. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? redraws the arrows for it.
interactive.ignores: The parts are ideal. A real coil's winding also has some resistance, which belongs in R, and a real capacitor wastes a little energy, so real parts sit slightly off straight up and straight down. The sliders move in small steps and readouts are rounded, so the frequency where the coil and capacitor cancel is shown as near a value. The two waves in the wave panel are drawn the same height to show their timing, not their sizes. Only parts in series are built here; parts side by side come in the next lesson.

explain.text:
A resistor, a coil and a capacitor each hold back an alternating current, and each one's opposition is counted in ohms. The difference is direction: on the complex plane the resistor's opposition lies along the real axis, the coil's points straight up and the capacitor's points straight down.[^1] Laid tip to tail, they make one complex number, Z = R + jX, called the [[impedance]]: the AC version of resistance, still in ohms.[^4][^5]

Why the quarter turns? A resistor's voltage rises and falls in step with its current, so its opposition has no j part: 8 Ω is 8 + j0.[^6] A coil is different. Remember from Calculus fundamentals that a coil's voltage follows how fast its current changes, v = L di/dt. The current wave changes fastest as it crosses zero and stops changing for an instant at its peak. So the coil's voltage is biggest as the current crosses zero, and zero as the current peaks: its wave is the current's wave a quarter cycle earlier. Draw each wave as its turning arrow from Trigonometry. The arrows turn anticlockwise, so the voltage's arrow, a quarter cycle ahead, is the current's arrow turned a quarter turn anticlockwise and resized. The first lesson showed that a quarter turn anticlockwise is multiplying by j. So the coil turns its current into its voltage by multiplying by j and by its size in ohms, X_L, and its opposition points up: +jX_L. A capacitor is the other way round. Its current follows how fast its voltage changes, i = C dv/dt, so its current peaks a quarter cycle before its voltage. Its voltage's arrow is the current's arrow turned a quarter turn back, clockwise, which is multiplying by −j, so its opposition points down: −jX_C. The size, X_L or X_C in ohms, is called [[reactance]]. A calculator's sum gives only that size; you put on the +j or −j from the kind of part.

The sizes depend on the frequency f. Double f and the current wave climbs twice as steeply, so a coil's voltage doubles for the same current: its reactance is X_L = 2πfL, growing in step with f.[^7] For a capacitor, a voltage wave twice as steep drives twice the current, so its opposition halves: X_C = 1 ÷ (2πfC),[^8] using ω = 2πf from Trigonometry, with L in henries and C in farads. At 50 Hz, the UK mains frequency,[^2] a 19.1 mH coil has X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.0191 = 6.0 Ω, and a 318 µF capacitor has X_C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 0.000318) = 10.0 Ω. At 100 Hz they become 12.0 Ω and 5.0 Ω. At very high frequencies a capacitor's reactance tends to zero, and it barely holds back the current at all.[^9]

With no coil or capacitor, X is 0 and Z is just R, your DC resistance. In series the parts still add, as resistors in series do, but now as arrows, tip to tail as in the adding lesson: Z = R + jX_L − jX_C = R + j(X_L − X_C). An 8 Ω resistor with that 6 Ω coil gives Z = 8 + j6. In polar form its length is √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 and its angle is tan⁻¹(6 ÷ 8) = 36.87°, so Z = 10∠36.87°. That is 10 Ω, not 8 + 6 = 14 Ω, because the coil's 6 Ω stands at a quarter turn to the 8. The right-angled triangle of R, X and Z is called the [[impedance triangle]]. Add the 10 Ω capacitor and Z = 8 + j(6 − 10) = 8 − j4, which is 8.94∠−26.57°: the capacitor's arrow is longer, so Z dips below the real axis. Raise f and the coil's arrow grows while the capacitor's shrinks; near 65 Hz they cancel, and Z is the 8 Ω resistor alone. One power-systems text, a secondary source, notes that Z's angle φ is also the angle between the voltage across the parts and the current through them,[^10] so cos φ is the power factor from Trigonometry: cos 36.87° = 0.8. The next lesson shows why. Z is not a phasor, because a phasor stands for a voltage or a current;[^11] at any one frequency, Z is a fixed opposition that does not turn with the wave. These are ideal parts: a real coil's winding adds a little resistance to R. **Impedance is resistance with an angle, all in ohms: the resistor's part lies along the real axis, the coil's points up and the capacitor's points down, and in series they add tip to tail.[^4][^1]**

analogy.text: Think of the power triangle from Trigonometry. A load's true power in kW is the side along the bottom, its reactive power in kVAr stands at a quarter turn to it, and the apparent power in kVA is the long side, so 8 kW with 6 kVAr is 10 kVA, not 14. The impedance triangle has the same shape: R along the bottom, X up or down, Z the long side, and the same angle φ.
analogy.breaks: The power triangle counts power, which grows as more current flows, while the impedance triangle counts ohms, which stay the same whatever the current. The shapes match for a reason you can work out: true power is P = I²R and reactive power is Q = I²X, so the power triangle is the impedance triangle with every side multiplied by I². That is why the two share their angle φ but not their sizes.

practice.text:
- Work out each reactance at the working frequency: X_L = 2πfL and X_C = 1 ÷ (2πfC). Put L in henries (mH ÷ 1000) and C in farads (µF ÷ 1000000).
- Give each part its direction: the resistor R, the coil +jX_L, the capacitor −jX_C.
- In series, add them: Z = R + j(X_L − X_C).
- For polar form, sketch it, then length √(R² + X²) and angle tan⁻¹(X ÷ R), where X = X_L − X_C (if R is 0, the angle is +90° or −90°).
- Read the angle: positive means the coil wins and Z points up; negative means the capacitor wins and Z points down. Its cosine is the power factor.

**Rule of thumb:** Coil up, capacitor down. Raise the frequency and the coil's arrow grows while the capacitor's shrinks.

**Rule of thumb:** Sizes at a quarter turn combine by Pythagoras, not by adding: 8 Ω with a 6 Ω coil is 10 Ω.

**Worked example:** Model a coil on 50 Hz as 12 Ω of winding resistance in series with 50.9 mH. X_L = 2π × 50 × 0.0509 = 16.0 Ω, so Z = 12 + j16. Its length is √(144 + 256) = √400 = 20 Ω and its angle tan⁻¹(16 ÷ 12) = 53.13°, so Z = 20∠53.13°, pointing up because the coil wins. The power factor is cos 53.13° = 0.6. On a ship the supply is different: MIT's notes say most ships at sea run at 60 Hz,[^3] so a coil of 6 Ω there takes L = 6 ÷ (2π × 60) = 0.0159 H, or 15.9 mH, not the 19.1 mH it takes on 50 Hz mains.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing a reactance without its direction. A 10 Ω capacitor is −j10, not 10 or +j10.
- Adding the sizes. 8 Ω with a 6 Ω coil is 10 Ω, not 14 Ω, nor 8 − 6 = 2 Ω.
- Adding the capacitor's reactance to the coil's instead of taking it away. 8 + j6 − j10 is 8 − j4.
- Using mH or µF straight in the formula. Turn them into henries and farads first.
- Thinking both reactances grow with frequency. The coil's grows; the capacitor's shrinks.

checks.label: Resistive impedance has a phase angle of zero degrees, so its vector points to the right, while inductive impedance with its 90° phase angle points up and capacitive impedance with its −90° phase angle points down: on every screen, in every answer and at every builder setting tested, the resistor's arrow points right along the real axis, the coil's straight up and the capacitor's straight down

Reactance is computed as XL = 2πfL: at every builder setting tested (R 0, 8 and 20 Ω; L 0, 19.1 and 40 mH; C 100, 318 and 1000 µF; f 20, 50, 65, 100 and 150 Hz) the coil's arrow is 2πfL ohms long, with L in henries, to 0.1 Ω, and starts at the resistor's tip
X_C = 1/ωC is the capacitive reactance, with ω = 2πf: at every builder setting tested the capacitor's arrow is 1 ÷ (2πfC) ohms long, with C in farads, to 0.1 Ω, and starts at the coil's tip

At very high frequencies, the capacitor's reactance tends to zero: on the builder each step up in frequency leaves the capacitor's arrow no longer and the coil's no shorter, and at the top of the frequency range the capacitor's is far shorter than at the bottom
The mains supply in the UK is an alternating current at a frequency of 50 hertz: the builder opens at 50 Hz, where its 19.1 mH coil comes to 6.0 Ω and its 318 µF capacitor to 10.0 Ω

Impedance is the ac analog to resistance and measures the combined effect of resistance, capacitive reactance and inductive reactance: at every builder setting tested Z's arrow runs from 0 to the capacitor's tip, R + j(X_L − X_C), and where the coil's and capacitor's reactances are equal Z is R alone
Z = 6 + j0 for a pure resistance and Z = 0 + j4 for a pure reactance: drawn by the builder's rule, the first lies along the real axis and the second points straight up

Known answers worked by hand: at 50 Hz 19.1 mH is 6.0 Ω and 318 µF is 10.0 Ω, at 100 Hz 12.0 Ω and 5.0 Ω; 8 + j6 − j10 = 8 − j4; 8 + j6 = 10∠36.87°, power factor 0.8; 8 − j4 = 8.94∠−26.57°, power factor 0.89; the builder at 100 Hz gives 8 + j7.0; 10∠36.87° = 8 + j6; 5∠−53.13° = 3 − j4; 6 + j8 = 10∠53.13°, 6 + j4 = 7.21∠33.69°, 6 + j2 = 6.32∠18.43°; the slips give 14, 2, 8 + j16 and 24

Each puzzle takes only its right answer: its three answers differ, the right one matches a working done separately here and only it is drawn without a mistake; each wrong one is drawn as what its slip makes, in red
Before an answer, a puzzle shows only its question: no working, no voltage wave and nothing marked as a mistake
Every demonstration finishes within 4.8 s of its screen opening and none starts before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 3 s

Raising the frequency lengthens the coil's arrow, shortens the capacitor's and swings Z from below the real axis to above it: at the opening settings, for every whole hertz from 50 to 100, the drawn coil never shortens, the capacitor never lengthens and Z's angle never falls, crossing the real axis between 64 and 66 Hz; the frequency demonstration ends at 100 Hz with Z above the axis

A coil's voltage peaks a quarter cycle before its current: on the wave screen the voltage wave, its arrow a quarter turn ahead, peaks at 360°, the current's at 450°, and the bracket spans those 90°, a quarter of the 360° cycle

From outside the rule: the practice coil, 12 Ω of winding with 50.9 mH on 50 Hz, has X_L = 16.0 Ω and Z = 12 + j16 = 20∠53.13°, power factor 0.6; the power triangle's 8 kW with 6 kVAr is 10 kVA, not 14; and a coil and capacitor cancel where 2πfL = 1 ÷ (2πfC), at f = 1 ÷ (2π√(LC)), which for 19.1 mH and 318 µF is near 65 Hz

applied.problem: Z is said to be 'a fixed opposition' right after the lesson shows it changing with frequency; it is fixed only at one frequency. Also the voltage arrow is the current's arrow resized by X_L (volts vs amps, can be shorter), not always 'stretched'.
'angle tan⁻¹(X ÷ R)' leaves X undefined in the practice (it is the net X_L − X_C) and fails at R = 0, which the resistance slider allows: a pure coil or capacitor sits at +90° or −90°.
